title: Like his father
hook: Marcus on his adoptive father Antoninus: steady, unhurried, finishing what he began (Meditations 1.16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the reed said its secret is near its lament. Your line was listen to the lament. Did you count to three before answering someone? Day one hundred sixty-nine.

Some people make a room calmer just by walking into it. They don't talk much. They don't rush. When they say they'll do something, it gets done, and nobody hears about it. You might have had a grandparent like that, or a coach, or a nurse on a night shift. Marcus Aurelius had one. Not his birth father, who died when he was small, but the man who adopted him and raised him to rule: the emperor Antoninus. In book one, when Marcus reaches him, the list of debts suddenly turns into the longest portrait in the book. Today, like his father.
screen: `THEY MAKE A ROOM CALMER.` → `THE MAN WHO ADOPTED HIM.` → `LIKE HIS FATHER.`

segments.voice: Antoninus ruled Rome for twenty-three years, from 138 to 161, and it was one of the quietest reigns the empire ever had. He adopted Marcus as a teenager, as part of the plan for who would come next, and Marcus lived beside him for years, watching. What he saw, he wrote down in Meditations 1.16. It opens, in George Long's translation: "In my father I observed mildness of temper, and unchangeable resolution in the things which he had determined after due deliberation." Mild, and immovable. Gentle, but once he'd thought it through, he finished it. The portrait goes on for a long page. He wasn't vain about honors. He listened to anyone who had something useful to say. He looked into things carefully in council and didn't settle for first impressions. He was content with little, and cheerful. He took care of his body without fussing over it. He never did anything in a rush, or so it looked, but everything got done, in order, without strain. Later in the notebook, Marcus tells himself to do everything as a student of Antoninus would. And there's a story, told by an ancient biography that isn't always reliable, that on the day he died Antoninus gave the palace guard their watchword for the night, and the word was equanimity. Whether or not it happened, it fits the man Marcus remembered. Here's the lesson for us, who mostly live on hurry. Steadiness isn't slowness. It's doing one thing all the way, without panic, and then the next. Your line: unhurried, finished.
screen: `ANTONINUS: TWENTY-THREE QUIET YEARS.` · `MILD, AND IMMOVABLE WHEN DECIDED.` · `NOTHING RUSHED, EVERYTHING DONE.` · `THE LAST WATCHWORD: EQUANIMITY.` · then, large: `UNHURRIED, FINISHED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish one thing without hurry. Pick something small that's waiting: a dish, a drawer, an email, a bed to make. Settle, breathe, and then do just that one thing, all the way to the end. Move at the speed of someone who has plenty of time, even if you don't. When your mind jumps ahead, come back to your hands. When it's done, notice it's done, and let yourself feel it. The bell holds the time.
Like his father. Marcus's portrait of Antoninus in Meditations 1.16: mild, steady, never rushed, finishing what he began. Today's word.
Your line: unhurried, finished. Today, choose one task and do it all the way through without switching to anything else, the way Antoninus would. Day one hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often return to Marcus's portrait of Antoninus (1.16) as a picture of steady character, and some modern Stoics choose a real person they admire and ask what that person would do.

fork.setup: you're Antoninus, dying. the palace guard comes to ask for the night's watchword. what do you give them?
fork.reveal: in the story, his last watchword was equanimity, aequanimitas. the source isn't always reliable, but it fits the steady man Marcus remembered.

original.note: Latin: equanimity, an even mind. the watchword Antoninus is said to have given on his last day.

trapdoor: what you thought: a son praising his dad.
what it means: a detailed portrait of steady character, from a man who watched it up close for years.
what a scholar hears: Meditations 1.16, the longest section of book one; the aequanimitas watchword comes from the Historia Augusta, a late and uneven source.

sources.quoted: In my father I observed mildness of temper, and unchangeable resolution in the things which he had determined after due deliberation

notes: Long 1862, Meditations 1.16 opening: confirm exact wording.
Paraphrased traits from 1.16 (not vain about honors, listened to anyone useful, careful in council, content with little, cared for body without fuss, nothing done in haste): confirm.
6.30 ('do everything as a disciple of Antoninus'): paraphrased; confirm.
Aequanimitas watchword: Historia Augusta, Antoninus Pius 12.6; flagged as an uneven source.
Adoption: Hadrian arranged in 138 that Antoninus adopt Marcus (aged 16/17). Confirm 'as a teenager'.
